passage:
Zeenat,
I'm writing this instead of texting because texting is kind of the problem.
Last Saturday you didn't reply for three hours and I checked my phone about fifty times. By the time you answered, I'd already decided you were bored of me. So I posted that photo with a friend from tuition just to see if you'd get jealous. That was a test, and it wasn't fair to you.
Here's what I'm trying now. When the dread starts, I put the phone in the drawer, go for a run round the colony, and tell myself: no reply is not a no. It works a little better each time.
I really like being close to you. I just don't want my panic to crowd us.
Pranav

qa.q: How long did Zeenat take to reply last Saturday?
qa.a: Zeenat didn't reply for three hours.

qa.q: What was Pranav afraid of during those three hours?
qa.a: Pranav feared that Zeenat had become bored and was pulling away, which is why the checking felt so urgent.

qa.q: What turning point does Pranav describe, and why might it help?
qa.a: Pranav now puts the phone in a drawer and goes for a run when the dread starts, which calms the panic before it turns into another test.

qa.q: How might Zeenat have felt seeing the photo that was posted as a test?
qa.a: Zeenat may have felt confused or hurt at being tested without knowing why, which is why Pranav calls it unfair.

grounding: A teenager admits to constant message-checking, dread at a slow reply and a jealousy test, and describes learning to calm down alone.

passage: Didi, you're the only one I can tell this to. So Manoj and I have been talking for two months. When he's online and doesn't reply, my chest goes tight, like something's wrong. Last week I sent him six messages in ten minutes. Six! Then I told him Sameer from class had asked me out, which isn't even true, just to see if he'd care. He went quiet for a whole day and I felt awful. Now I've made a rule. When I want to send a second message, I stop, make chai, and text you instead. And yesterday I told Manoj straight, "I get scared when you don't reply. Can you just say busy?" He said okay. Honestly, didi, the Indu from last week would never.

qa.q: How many messages did Indu send in ten minutes?
qa.a: Indu sent six messages in ten minutes.

qa.q: What does Indu's tight chest suggest when Manoj is online but silent?
qa.a: It suggests Indu feels dread that something is wrong between them, even without any real sign.

qa.q: What new rule helps Indu, and why?
qa.a: Before a second message, Indu stops, makes chai and texts didi instead, which calms the alarm long enough to think.

qa.q: How might Manoj have felt when he heard the made-up story about Sameer?
qa.a: He was likely hurt or confused, which may be why he went quiet for a whole day.

grounding: A teenager confides dread at unanswered messages and a jealousy test, then describes pausing to self-soothe and asking directly.

passage:
Trisha,
I'm writing this instead of texting, because texting is kind of the problem. On Friday, when you didn't answer for two hours, I checked my phone maybe forty times. I made up a whole story: you were bored of me, you liked someone from your art class. So I posted that photo with Kunal's arm round my shoulder, hoping you'd see it and feel what I felt. That was a test, and it wasn't fair. You were at your nani's with no signal. I'm trying something the school counsellor suggested: when the dread starts, I put the phone in a drawer, walk round the block and ask what I actually know. I really like you. I don't want to smother this.
Sarika

qa.q: Where was Trisha on Friday?
qa.a: At her nani's, with no signal.

qa.q: What was Sarika feeling during the two hours without a reply?
qa.a: Sarika felt dread and jealousy, imagining Trisha was bored or liked someone else, and checked the phone about forty times.

qa.q: What small step is Sarika trying for next time?
qa.a: Putting the phone in a drawer, walking round the block and asking what is actually known before reacting.

qa.q: How might Trisha have felt seeing the photo with Kunal?
qa.a: Trisha was probably confused and hurt, having done nothing wrong except being somewhere with no signal.

grounding: Shows a teen who checks messages constantly, dreads a delayed reply and tests a partner with jealousy, then learns to self-soothe.

passage: Okay, don't laugh. You know how Dhruv takes forever to reply? Last week he saw my message at 8:14 and said nothing until ten. I'm Neelam, I'm fifteen, and I spent those two hours refreshing the screen like a crazy person, sure he'd found someone better. Then I did something dumb. I told him Aman from tuition had offered to walk me home, just to see if he'd care. He did care. He got upset, and I felt awful, because all I really wanted was for him to say he missed me. So now I've got a rule. When my stomach does that drop, I put on music and sketch for twenty minutes before I touch the phone. Mostly he's replied by then. And if he hasn't, I'm calmer anyway.

qa.q: When did Dhruv see Neelam's message?
What was Neelam really wanting when the story about Aman came out?
qa.a: Neelam wanted closeness and reassurance, hoping Dhruv would say he missed Neelam, but the test only led to feeling awful.

qa.q: How does Neelam's new rule help?
qa.a: Sketching to music for twenty minutes gives the panic time to settle, so Neelam doesn't act on the fear.

qa.q: How might Dhruv have felt hearing about Aman?
qa.a: Dhruv likely felt jealous and upset, not knowing it was a test.

grounding: Illustrates a teen who dreads delayed replies, tests with jealousy and then learns a way to self-soothe.

passage:
Monday: Yusuf's reply took three hours, and Sarika spent them flipping her phone face-up, face-down on the desk, homework untouched. When he finally wrote, "sorry, cricket practice," she typed back "k" and posted a picture of herself laughing with his friend Omar, to see if he'd notice.
Thursday: The dread came again during a free period. This time Sarika wrote the feeling in the back of her notebook, "scared he's losing interest", and went to the canteen with her cousin.
The next Sunday: She told Yusuf plainly, "When you go quiet I panic a bit. Can you just say if you're busy?" He sent "busy, talk at 7" that evening, and called at seven. She went back to her book.

qa.q: What did Sarika write in the back of her notebook?
qa.a: "scared he's losing interest"

qa.q: Why did Sarika post the picture with Omar on Monday?
qa.a: She was anxious and jealous after the long silence and wanted to test whether Yusuf would notice and care.

qa.q: Which change helped Sarika most, and why?
qa.a: Naming the fear on paper and then asking Yusuf directly, because it calmed the panic and got her a simple answer.

qa.q: How might Yusuf see Sarika's Sunday message?
qa.a: He probably finds it easy to agree, because a clear request is simpler than guessing why she sent "k".

grounding: Shows over several days a teen moving from anxious checking and jealousy tests to self-soothing and asking directly.

passage:
Tejas, put the phone face down for a minute and listen to your Ganga Masi.
When I was sixteen, there was a boy called Sunil. We had those small phones then, only texts. If he didn't reply in ten minutes, my stomach dropped. I'd check the phone under my pillow, in the bathroom, during prayers. Once, when he went quiet for an evening, I told him another boy had walked me home. It wasn't even true. I just wanted him to feel as scared as I did.
He was hurt, and we nearly broke up.
That night I made myself a small rule. When the dread came, I would write it in my diary first, then call my friend Lata or walk round the colony. Only after that could I text him.
It was hard. Some nights I wrote three pages. But the texts I sent after were kinder, and so was I.

qa.q: Where did young Ganga check her phone?
qa.a: Under her pillow, in the bathroom and during prayers.

qa.q: How did young Ganga feel when Sunil didn't reply?
qa.a: She felt dread and fear; her stomach dropped if he didn't reply in ten minutes, and she wanted him to feel as scared as she did.

qa.q: What choice did young Ganga make after nearly breaking up, and why did it help?
qa.a: She decided to write in her diary, call Lata or walk before texting, which calmed the dread so her texts were kinder.

qa.q: How was Sunil affected when she invented the story about another boy?
qa.a: He was hurt by it, and they nearly broke up, because the jealousy test made him doubt her.

grounding: Shows an aunt recalling a teenage romance where she checked for replies, felt dread and tested with jealousy, then learned to soothe herself first.
